reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: The most common terminal (subtelomeric) deletion syndrome recognised in humans
Unlike the interstitial recurrent syndromes, most cases arise from de novo terminal deletions of variable size rather than recombination between segmental duplications
Infantile hypotonia, feeding difficulty and global developmental delay with usually severe intellectual disability and very limited or absent speech
Seizures are frequent and infantile spasms may occur
Structural congenital heart defects and, importantly, a cardiomyopathy (dilated or left ventricular non-compaction) that can present beyond the neonatal period
Characteristic facies with straight eyebrows, deep-set eyes, midface hypoplasia, a broad flat nasal bridge, pointed chin and small low-set ears
Sensory involvement is common, including hearing loss and visual problems, alongside behavioural features such as self-injurious behaviour
Chromosomal microarray reliably detects the deletion and defines its size
reference.pathophysiology: 1p36 deletion syndrome results from loss of the terminal short arm of chromosome 1. Most deletions occur de novo and vary considerably in size and breakpoint position, so the condition is best regarded as a contiguous-gene syndrome rather than a single recurrent rearrangement; unbalanced translocations and more complex rearrangements are also seen. Haploinsufficiency of several dosage-sensitive genes across the region impairs neuronal development and cardiac structure and function, with loss of genes influencing myocardial development contributing to the cardiomyopathy and congenital heart defects. The variability in deletion size partly explains the breadth of the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other subtelomeric or terminal deletion syndromes
Angelman syndrome (severe developmental delay, seizures, happy demeanour)
Rett syndrome and MECP2-related disorders in girls with regression and seizures
Other genetic causes of infantile-onset cardiomyopathy
Non-specific severe intellectual disability with epilepsy
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as the first-line test to detect and size the terminal deletion
FISH or MLPA to confirm the finding and assess for a parental rearrangement
Parental karyotype and studies to exclude a balanced translocation influencing recurrence risk
Echocardiography at diagnosis and on surveillance for congenital heart disease and cardiomyopathy
EEG where seizures are suspected and brain MRI for structural anomalies
redFlags: Signs of heart failure or newly detected cardiomyopathy
Significant feeding difficulty with faltering growth or aspiration risk
Apnoea or airway compromise in infancy
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have significant lifelong intellectual disability and require substantial support, and life expectancy can be reduced when serious cardiac disease or refractory epilepsy is present. Regular cardiac and developmental surveillance, seizure control and sensory support materially affect quality of life and outcome.
pitfalls: Overlooking cardiomyopathy, which may develop after infancy and requires ongoing cardiac surveillance rather than a single normal echocardiogram
Failing to arrange parental studies to identify an inherited translocation with recurrence implications
Attributing seizures solely to the deletion without appropriate neurological evaluation
Missing hearing or visual impairment that compounds developmental difficulty
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Provide developmental therapies — physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech-and-language input — with individualised educational support
Control seizures, including infantile spasms, with appropriate antiseizure medication such as vigabatrin or corticotrophin and corticosteroids for spasms
Undertake echocardiographic surveillance for congenital heart defects and cardiomyopathy, whether dilated or left-ventricular non-compaction, managing heart failure as it arises
Support feeding and nutrition in the hypotonic infant, using gastrostomy where oral intake is inadequate
Arrange hearing and ophthalmological assessment with appropriate sensory support
Offer genetic counselling with parental karyotype and studies to exclude a balanced translocation and to counsel recurrence risk
Coordinate lifelong care through a multidisciplinary neurodisability team
